frameworks.name: Three-Element Daily Excellence
frameworks.definition: A personal operating system anchored on three observable daily behaviors—workout with liked people, meal with liked people, write something down—that predicts subjective well-being and composable life quality.

frameworks.name: Life Stage and Organizational Focus Progression
frameworks.definition: A three-phase model where founder priorities shift from destination (20s) to journey (30s) to company and people (40s), driving decision architecture at each stage.

claims.text: The best talent available to scale a business lies in the future, not the past. Understanding why superior teams generate higher revenue requires observing demonstrable team quality differences, not just hearing assertions about capability.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Observing superior teams' output and margins demonstrates ROI of talent investment directly, making the hiring-as-capital-allocation mental model visceral rather than abstract.
bounded_by: Does not address early-stage single-founder hiring where demonstration capacity is limited

claims.text: Observing and demonstrating superior team quality (revenue generation, execution speed, output consistency) breaks founder beliefs about talent availability more effectively than verbal persuasion alone.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: The human brain updates mental models faster through observable evidence (seeing a high-performing team execute) than through claims without demonstration.

claims.text: Surrounding yourself with people you genuinely like significantly decreases days where business frustration or failure becomes unbearable, because liking the people you work with separates satisfaction-with-people from satisfaction-with-business-outcome.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: When business circumstances are negative, personal liking for colleagues provides an independent source of positive affect, mitigating overall job dissatisfaction.
bounded_by: Does not guarantee business success; addresses psychological sustainability only

claims.text: Days with three observable recurring behaviors—working out with liked people, eating with liked people, and writing something down—produce subjectively above-average life quality, and deliberately maximizing consecutive days with these three elements increases reported well-being.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: These three behaviors create observable daily structure and social connection that compound over repeated days, with feedback loops that naturally encourage addition of similar high-utility behaviors.

numbers.axis: daily presence of three behaviors (workout with liked people, meal with liked people, writing)

claims.text: Defining personal well-being by observable, measurable behaviors (rather than emotional states, identity claims, or abstract concepts like 'vibration' or 'energy') creates a falsifiable tracking system that compounds through iteration.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: person has capacity to observe and track behaviors
claims.mechanism: Observable definitions allow feedback loops—iteration, error correction, and compounding—because success/failure is measurable and repeatable.
bounded_by: Does not address clinical depression or severe mental health challenges where observable behavior alone is insufficient

examples.text: Alex Hormozi observed that his best-remembered and most-enjoyed days shared three elements: working out with people he liked, eating with people he liked, and writing something down. Over 100+ consecutive days of deliberately maximizing these three elements, the framework evolved—he noticed that on certain days, merely eating healthy food was insufficient; only eating with liked people satisfied the third element. This iterative refinement created a composite personal operating system that was both simple and compositionally robust.

When creativity is defined as mistakes that occur while copying (the mechanism by which nature produces innovation), deliberate iteration compounds toward better outcomes. An accidental example: cutting a potato slightly too thin during intended replication accidentally created potato chips, demonstrating that attempted copying with small failures produces novel value.

Sharon, the company president, articulated his own life-stage progression: in his 20s he cared about destination (end-goal achievement), in his 30s he cared about the journey (process quality), and in his 40s he cared about the company and people. This three-phase model shows how founder priorities naturally evolve when consciously observed.

practices.text: Track days subjectively rated as above average and identify the behavioral patterns (workout with liked people, meal with liked people, writing) with the highest frequency on those days.
Deliberately structure your schedule to maximize the likelihood that high-frequency good-day behaviors occur consistently.
When hiring and building teams, prioritize talent quality and demonstrate team capability to break founder beliefs about what is achievable, rather than relying on assertion alone.
Compose team membership around people you genuinely like working with, separating people-satisfaction from business-outcome satisfaction.
